findings.title: Regular Expression Denial of Service (ReDoS) in glob pattern translation
findings.explanation: Translator.translate_core()/replace() converts each literal '*' in a user-supplied glob pattern into the unbounded quantifier '[^<seps>]*' and leaves them concatenated with literal characters in between whenever they do not form a bare '**' segment (the only case guarded by restrict_rglob). A pattern such as '*a' repeated N times therefore compiles to the regex '([^/]*a){N}', which is the textbook catastrophic-backtracking shape: when matched against a filename that almost-but-not-quite satisfies it, the backtracking engine tries an exponential number of ways to split the string among the '[^/]*' groups before failing. Because Path.glob()/Path.rglob() (zipp/__init__.py) run this compiled regex with .fullmatch() against every name in the archive's filelist, any caller that forwards an externally influenced glob pattern into Path.glob()/rglob() (e.g. a service that lets a user search inside an uploaded or server-side zip archive) lets that user hang the process. This was verified experimentally: pattern ('*a'*25)+'!' (51 characters) matched against a 30-character filename inside a Path.glob() call took over 11 seconds of pure CPU time; the cost grows exponentially with the number of '*a' repetitions, so a slightly longer pattern (tens of bytes) is enough to make a single call run for hours, causing a complete denial of service with trivially small, fully attacker-controlled input.
